The -dl and -dg dumps give the whole mechanism: each product is one insn whose result prefers LO; the global allocator takes them by priority (r square 2 refs over 3 insns, dy square 2 over 4, dx square 2 over 10); the first gets LO, reload needs LO back and moves that one to a1 (a0 is skipped, the parameter prefers it), the second gets v1, the third a2. Retail has dy square in a1 and r square in v1, so dy square (or dx square) ranks first there. The order at allocation time is forced by v0 (dy, then r, then the sum): dy mult, r load, r mult, sum, compare. Only one more insn between the sum and the compare (a tie goes to the lower pseudo), a third reference to the dy square, or four references to the dx square flips it. tried: counter through a u16 local (n = count; n++; count = n) with the retail store order colour, count, x, B4, y: 18 rows, kept. Local allocation gives the counter the highest priority in the dot block (12 refs over 9 insns), so it takes v0 ahead of the colour (a multi-block value); retail has the counter in a1 and the dot pointer in a2, behind the x-chain values in v0, v1 and a0. Test: reusing n in the tail block makes it a multi-block value and the colour and D.x take v0 as in retail, with the counter in a2 and the dot in a1. So retail allocates the counter and the dot pointer in the global pass: each lives in more than one block there. Forms that keep them in one block cannot match (counter read before or after the dot, n + 1, += 1, x through a local, colour local)
